Patients on angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE)-inhibitors (ACE-I) presenting with chronic cough should be taken off the ACE-I regardless of temporal relationship to development of cough. C
Evaluation should begin with a CXR in all patients, as well as pulmonary function testing (PFT) in patients with suspected asthma. C

background.definition: Chronic cough is classically defined as cough >3 weeks' duration; however, post-upper respiratory infection (URI) bronchial irritation frequently lasts up to 7 weeks. Waiting to start evaluation for chronic cough until 6 to 8 weeks have passed in patients with a recent URI is therefore reasonable.

list.listitem: Prevalence of chronic cough is 14% to 23% in nonsmoking adults.
Chronic cough is reported in up to 9% of preschool-aged children.
More than $600 million a year is spent on over-the-counter and prescription medicines for cough.
More than 25.9 million primary care office visits annually are due to chronic cough as the chief complaint and most frequent symptom.
Ninety percent of patients with chronic cough are diagnosed with GERD, PND syndrome, and/or asthma.
Smoking.
Approximately 12% of patients taking ACE-I will develop cough.
An aberrant innominate artery may be indicated in infants up to 18 months old.
Chronic cough is a common component of long COVID or post-acute COVID syndrome.
For other causes, see Differential Diagnosis (below).
Chronic irritation in PND, GERD, and smoking.
Bronchospasm in asthma.
ACE-I decreasing breakdown of protussive substances.
Vagal nerve irritation.
Habit/psychogenic cough.
Ninety percent of patients with chronic cough have GERD, PND syndrome, and/or asthma; nearly two-thirds of patients will have more than one of these contributing to their cough. B
Evaluation should begin with a CXR, as well as PFTs in patients suspected of asthma. C
Consider additional testing for selected patients: PPD, chest CT, methylcholine provocation test, bronchoscopy, and/or 24-hour esophageal pH monitoring. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Erythema on rhinoscopy, allergic rhinitis symptoms
Sputum eosinophils with normal spirometry and CXR
Diagnosis of exclusion, r/o genetic tic disorder like Tourette
Fever, bloody sputum, night sweats, exposure
Symptoms beginning with acute COVID infection and persisting at least 2 months.

list.listitem: Evaluate adults with chronic cough for complete history of exposures to respiratory irritants, including cigarette, cigar, and pipe smoke; passive smoke exposures; and hazardous environments in the home and at work.

Inquire about recent URI, bronchitis, or pneumonia; bronchial irritation can last as long as 7 weeks. Consider pneumonia or acute exacerbation of COPD in patients with acute exacerbation of chronic cough.
Paroxysmal cough, post-tussive emesis, and a inspiratory "whoop" all suggest pertussis as the cause.
Ask about an allergic component: Is cough triggered by change in season or new exposure, or are there other allergic rhinitis symptoms? PND is the most common cause of chronic cough.
Ask about timing of cough. A cough worse at night may point to PND or GERD as causes.
Ask about exercise or exposure (pets, smoke, etc.) that triggered cough; consider cough variant asthma.
If starting ACE-I therapy, or in patients already taking an ACE-I with chronic cough, you can use a clinical rule to calculate ACE-I cough risk.
Cough may be triggered by cough receptors in eustachian tubes or sinuses, so consider "silent" otitis media as cause for cough, especially in children.
For chronic cough, especially in children, consider foreign body as cause for cough.

Adults with chronic cough and sputum production occurring most days for at least 3 months and for at least two consecutive years should be given a diagnosis of chronic bronchitis when other respiratory or cardiac causes of chronic productive cough are ruled out.
In immunocompromised hosts, consider opportunistic infections.
Evaluation should begin with CXR and pulmonary function testing (PFT), especially in smokers and persons suspected of having asthma or COPD.

In a study of 378 patients with chronic cough, 91% had erythema or abnormal discharge on rhinoscopy; 74% of those people had improved cough with 5-day treatment for PND with nasal steroid, decongestant, and antihistamine. In the same study, all patients with positive sputum eosinophil count and methacholine provocation test had improvement of cough with treatment with inhaled steroid and long-acting beta agonist.

Patients with positive sputum eosinophil count or methacholine bronchial provocation test (MPT) almost certainly have asthma contributing to chronic cough. MPT may also help diagnose asthmatic cough in patients without other signs/symptoms of asthma.

Consider 24-hour pH monitoring if equivocal response from empiric GERD therapy. Mean nocturnal baseline impedance (MNBI) and the postreflux swallow-induced peristaltic wave (PSPW) index both may increase the diagnostic yield of patients with chronic cough and suspected GERD.
Order PPD screening for tuberculosis in high-risk populations and in any patients with fever or night sweats.
Consider sinus CT if suspicious for chronic sinusitis as cause of cough.
Smokers with hemoptysis and normal CXR should have bronchoscopy to evaluate for malignancy.

listitem.strong: Evaluation of chronic cough (> 4 weeks) in children

list.listitem: As in adults, CHEST expert panel guidelines (2020) recommend that evaluation begins with CXR and pulmonary function testing.
Consider a test for airway hyperresponsiveness in children age 6 to 14 years and also testing for Bordetella pertussis if clinically suspected.
Do not routinely order skin prick test, Mantoux test, bronchoscopy, or chest CT unless clinically indicated.
A clinical decision rule to predict the likelihood of ACE-I cough has been developed and validated. Race (especially East Asian), female sex, age over 60, and history of cough are important factors.
Begin evaluation with a CXR pulmonary function testing in both children and adults with chronic unexplained cough.
Stop ACE-I in patients taking these drugs, or switch to alternate drug.
Empiric therapy based on most-likely presumptive diagnosis is the best approach for nonsmoking adults not taking an ACE-I ().
Consider additional testing for selected patients: PPD, chest CT, methylcholine provocation test, bronchoscopy, and/or 24-hour esophageal pH monitoring.
A detailed set of algorithms is provided by the CHEST expert panel guidelines for children with chronic cough.
In nonsmoking adults not taking an ACE-I treat PND, asthma, and GERD in stepwise fashion based on accompanying symptoms. Re-evaluate every 1 to 2 weeks until cough resolves. C

Patients on ACE-I presenting with chronic cough should be taken off the medication regardless of the temporal relationship between cough and initiation of drug. If ACE-I is cause, cough should typically resolve in 1 to 4 weeks after stopping the offending agent, though resolution may be delayed up to 3 months. C
There is little evidence to support the effectiveness of any treatment for subacute cough that is secondary to prior URI. C
See algorithm in to guide treatment of PND, GERD and asthma.
About 3 in 4 people with erythema or abnormal discharge on rhinoscopy will improve within 5 days of treatment with nasal steroid, decongestants, and antihistamine.

Treatment for GERD in patients with chronic cough may be effective in some patients. However, there is insufficient evidence to definitely conclude that treatment with PPI is universally beneficial for cough associated with GERD in adults. Data in children are inconclusive.

In a small study of patients with chronic cough due to postviral vagal neuropathy, low-dose amitriptyline increased quality of life (QOL) scores and majority of patients taking it achieved complete response.

Patients on ACE-I presenting with chronic cough should be taken off ACE-I regardless of temporal relationship of drug and cough development. However, a meta-analysis of 22 placebo-controlled RCTs suggested that two-thirds of coughs developing in patients on ACE-I are not due to the medication. If ACE-I is the cause, cough should resolve in 1 to 4 weeks after stopping the offending agent, though resolution may be delayed up to 3 months in some. If ACE-I is indicated, it is reasonable to try another ACE-I.

Treatment of URI with naproxen has a beneficial effect on the symptoms of headache, malaise, myalgia, and cough. Otherwise, there is relatively little good evidence regarding the effectiveness of over the counter cough preparations.

Inhaled steroids are helpful in cough due to asthma and nonasthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis. They are not helpful in nonasthmatic adults with cough due to lower respiratory tract infections. A Cochrane review of 8 RCTs found inconsistent results and significant heterogeneity in the studies to support the use of inhaled corticosteroids for adults with subacute and chronic cough.
For children with chronic cough not otherwise explained, a trial of inhaled steroids is an option.
Postinfectious cough may improve with ipratropium or inhaled steroids. Montelukast has also been used anecdotally for postinfectious cough.

Children under 12 years should not be prescribed codeine-based medications for chronic cough given the lack of RCTs to support this therapy, along with risks of adverse events including opioid toxicity and respiratory suppression.
Patients with cough from idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or sarcoidosis may have symptom improvement with inhaled corticosteroids, but there is no improvement with mortality or in QOL scores.
For patients with intractable cough, a small study found that morphine was effective.
A 2 week course of antibiotics is recommended for the treatment of children with chronic wet or moist cough. Antibiotic use must be balanced against known adverse events.

A single dose of buckwheat honey 30 minutes prior to bed improved cough better than honey-flavored dextromethorphan or placebo in children 2 to 18 years old with acute cough. A meta-analysis of two trials found honey to relieve cough frequency better than diphenhydramine but not dextromethorphan.
Air-modification interventions are not helpful in the treatment of prolonged, nonspecific cough in children.
There is insufficient to evaluate the efficacy of speech and language therapy in the treatment of adults with idiopathic or refractory chronic cough.
If no response after diagnosis/empiric treatment algorithm, consider referral to pulmonology.
Follow-up every 1 to 2 weeks is recommended to initiate next step in evaluation and empiric treatment until cough is improved. C
Stepwise treatment of chronic cough using algorithm will successfully treat chronic cough in 90% of patients: 50% in 5 days and greater than 80% within 12 days. B

Children with chronic cough should have CXR and spirometry for initial evaluation. If these tests are equivocal and the child has productive cough, bronchiectasis (cystic fibrosis) and immune deficiencies should be ruled out.

Placebo works just as well as either dextromethorphan or diphenhydramine to decrease cough frequency or severity in children. Active drugs provided no additional benefit on parents' report of their own or their child's sleep.

Beclomethasone dipropionate (400 mcg/d) is no different from placebo in reducing the frequency of cough measured objectively or scored subjectively. There might be a small improvement with very high-dose inhaled corticosteroid, but the clinical impact of this is likely to be small.
A 2 week course of antibiotics is recommended for the treatment of children with chronic wet or moist cough. Antibiotic use must be balanced against known adverse events.
Salbutamol is no different than placebo in reducing the frequency of cough measured objectively or scored subjectively.

There is no evidence to support the use of antihistamines, inhaled chromones, inhaled anticholinergics, methylxanthines, or leukotriene receptor antagonists in treating children with chronic nonspecific cough.
There is no evidence to support air-modification interventions in the treatment of prolonged, nonspecific cough in children.
Interventions targeting obstructive sleep apnea to treat chronic cough in children are not supported by RCTs.
Honey effectively decreases cough severity and sleep disruption in children. Do not give to infants due to concerns over botulism.

In a RCT of 272 children without known chronic respiratory illness, an algorithm-driven approach to early (2 weeks) referral to respiratory specialists was more effective at resolving chronic cough than delayed (6 weeks) referral.

cell.label: If smoker, advise smoking cessation, consider PFTs.
If COPD or if asthma clinically suspected, consider PFTs.
On ACE-I? Discontinue medications. Improved in 1 to 2 weeks?
Erythema on rhinoscopy or no other obvious cause for cough. Treat for PND. Improved in 1 to 2 weeks?
Treat for asthma with trial of inhaled steroid and beta agonist. Improved in 1 to 2 weeks?
Treat for GERD. Improved in 1 to 2 weeks?
Stop medications. Consider PPD, high-resolution chest CT, 24-hour esophageal pH monitoring, bronchoscopy, or referral to pulmonologist.
